organizingIdeas.title: Text Forms and Structures
organizingIdeas.statement: Identifying and applying text forms and structures improves understanding of content, literary style, and our rich language traditions.

guidingQuestions.question: How can text organization influence communication?

outcomes.outcome: Students examine how the form and structure of texts can support the communication of ideas and information.

knowledge.text: Fictional texts can be categorized by sub-genres, including fantasy.
A fantasy is a fictional text that contains elements that are highly unreal.
Fictional texts can have structures that include main plots with subplots and flashbacks.
A flashback interrupts the story plot to take an audience back in time to past events in a character’s life.

A minor character is a character in a story who is not the main focus and is less developed.
Fictional texts include characters who can be known by what they say, think, or do.
Point of view is the way an author or a text creator chooses to tell or narrate a story and includes first person.
First person is where the author, text creator, or narrator relates information from their own point of view, often by using the word I.

understanding.text: Fictional texts can open minds to new possibilities and ideas.

organizingIdeas.title: Oral Language
organizingIdeas.statement: Listening and speaking form the foundation for literacy development and improve communication, collaboration, and respectful mutual understanding.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can listening and speaking skills clarify intent and build relationships?

outcomes.outcome: Students examine and demonstrate how listening and speaking support connections and clarify understandings.

knowledge.text: Oral traditions can support connections to
Stories presented in oral traditions can reflect connections to spirit, land, universe, time, and people.
Protocols for sharing information may vary by source, context, community, or culture.

understanding.text: Oral traditions can connect the speaker and listener to experiences of the past or present that help prepare for the future.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Describe personal connections to spirit, land, the universe, time, or people revealed through oral traditions.
Discuss protocols used to share oral traditions.

knowledge.text: Respectful interactions include behaviours that consider the contributions, feelings, points of view, and needs of participants.

knowledge.text: Projection is the directing and supporting of the voice toward an intended target.
Projection is a combination of breath, clarity, and intentionality.

understanding.text: Listening and speaking skills can be applied and adapted to support respectful interactions.

knowledge.text: Listening includes restating key points or ideas and making personal connections.

understanding.text: Listening involves playing an active role in understanding the speaker and supports collaboration.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Demonstrate active listening when engaging in collaborative work.

organizingIdeas.title: Vocabulary
organizingIdeas.statement: Communication and comprehension are improved by understanding word meaning and structures.

guidingQuestions.question: How can building vocabulary and understanding morphology strengthen communication?

outcomes.outcome: Students expand vocabulary and analyze morphemes to communicate in multiple contexts.

Personification is when animals or objects are given qualities or abilities that a human can have.
An analogy compares two things that are mostly different but have some things in common.
An idiom is a phrase that means something different than the literal meaning of the words within it.

understanding.text: An extensive and varied vocabulary enhances effective communication in a variety of contexts.

organizingIdeas.title: Fluency
organizingIdeas.statement: Comprehension and literary appreciation are improved by the ability to read a range of texts accurately, automatically, and with expression.

guidingQuestions.question: How does fluency support comprehension and proficient reading?

outcomes.outcome: Students enhance fluency to refine comprehension and proficient reading.

knowledge.text: Proficient reading involves the ability to read with accuracy, automaticity, and prosody with a focus on meaning.

understanding.text: Reading with fluency allows readers to focus more attention on understanding text and supports proficient reading.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Demonstrate comprehension of text through appropriate stress on words, pausing, phrasing, intonation, and use of punctuation.
Read dialogue with phrasing and expression to reflect understandings of characters and events.

organizingIdeas.title: Comprehension
organizingIdeas.statement: Text comprehension is supported by applying varied strategies and processes and by considering both particular contexts and universal themes.

guidingQuestions.question: How do comprehension processes and strategies enhance understandings of texts?

outcomes.outcome: Students investigate strategies and connections that support text comprehension.

knowledge.text: A variety of reading processes and strategies support comprehension of longer and more complex texts through independent practice.

understanding.text: Comprehension processes and strategies can be purposefully applied to broaden understandings of texts.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Independently read and demonstrate comprehension of a variety of texts that increase in length or complexity.
Apply comprehension processes and strategies when interacting with texts.

knowledge.text: Connections that support comprehension of text include

understanding.text: Comprehension is enhanced when relevant connections are made to information within and between texts.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Examine connections between texts and self, between a text and other texts, and between texts and the world.
Compare or contrast aspects of texts within an individual text or between multiple texts.
Reflect on personal connections to a text that best support understandings.

understanding.text: Comprehension and making predictions have a reciprocal relationship when understanding texts.

understanding.text: Comprehension involves inferencing and relying on multiple critical-thinking skills when engaging with texts.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Infer cause-and-effect relationships in texts.

knowledge.text: Summarizing information involves determining key ideas and specific details, logically ordering ideas, and paraphrasing.
Synthesizing can create new understandings through a combination of background knowledge and new information from a text.

understanding.text: Comprehension is enhanced when information is synthesized and summarized.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Synthesize a variety of information when creating summaries of texts.

organizingIdeas.title: Writing
organizingIdeas.statement: Ideas and information can be articulated accurately and imaginatively through the use of writing processes and an understanding of the author’s craft.

guidingQuestions.question: How can development of writing processes and expression support effective communication?

outcomes.outcome: Students construct and organize text to share perspectives and develop creative expression.

Methods and tools that support planning include
Interest can be created by varying sentence beginnings and lengths.
Paragraphs include a topic sentence, supporting details, and a concluding sentence.
A topic sentence describes what the paragraph is going to be about.
A concluding sentence brings closure to a paragraph by identifying main ideas without adding new information.
Fluent writing is smooth, natural, and easy to read aloud with inflection, which helps bring out meaning.
Revising includes adding or removing words or sentences to enhance writing clarity or fluency.
Publishing can involve consideration and selection of a variety of text features to enhance and finalize written work.

understanding.text: Writing is a vehicle for communication, creativity, and connection.

organizingIdeas.title: Conventions
organizingIdeas.statement: Understanding grammar, spelling, and punctuation makes it easier to communicate clearly, to organize thinking, and to use language for desired effects.

guidingQuestions.question: How does the knowledge and application of conventions enhance written communication?

outcomes.outcome: Students examine and apply conventions to develop effective written communication.

knowledge.text: Capitalization is used for abbreviations.
An abbreviation is the shortened form of a word or words (e.g., Rd., St., AB).
Punctuation can be used to add clarity, precision, or creativity to messages.
A comma can have a variety of uses, including
items: to indicate a pause between parts of a sentence
to separate words in a list or series
to separate a transition word from the words that follow in a sentence

understanding.text: Capitalization and punctuation can be used to support writing fluency.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Capitalize words appropriately in different contexts.
Include a variety of punctuation at the end of sentences.
Insert commas to indicate a pause between parts of sentences, to separate items in a list, or to follow a transition word.
Insert quotation marks to identify the words of a speaker or to bring attention to a word that is used in a special way.
Insert apostrophes in place of letters in contractions and to show possession.

knowledge.text: Sentences can describe facts or actions happening in the present (present tense).
Sentences can describe what happened in the past (past tense).
Sentences can describe what may happen in the future (future tense).
The subject of a verb is the person or thing that performs the action.
The object of a verb is the person or thing that receives the action.
Both subjects and objects can be nouns or pronouns.
Pronouns can replace a noun as the subject of a sentence (subjective) (e.g., I, you, he, she, it, we, they).
Possessive adjectives come before a noun to show who or what owns it (e.g., my, your, his, her, its, our, their).
Adjectives can compare two things (comparative—<er> or “more”).
Adjectives can compare three or more things (superlative—<est> or “most”).

understanding.text: Grammatical structures can support consistency in communication.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Distinguish between a variety of sentence types.

Use adjectives to indicate comparison of two or more things (<er> or <est>).
Use conjunctions to connect phrases in sentences.
Apply consistent subject-verb agreement in a variety of sentences.

understanding.text: Guidelines for spelling transferred to writing new text can increase written clarity.
